events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Priya proposes Priya, Isha. As leader I'll take responsibility on the first mission and pair myself with Isha, who has given no cause for concern. A small early team builds trust and keeps the proposal uncontroversial.

A two-person team on Mission 1 is straightforward enough, but I'd like to think carefully before voting. Priya, you're proposing yourself alongside Isha — as first leader that's a natural pick, but I'd want to hear why Isha specifically feels like the right partner here rather than one of the other three of us. On a small team, both seats matter a lot. Isha, since your name is on the line too, how do you feel about being picked for this first mission?

Thanks, Noah. Being picked feels fine to me. I have no special information, so I can't vouch for anyone beyond what we've seen so far. Priya's reason is simple: a two-person first team keeps the risk low, and as leader she's taking responsibility for it. I'd like to hear from Zara and Omar before we vote, especially whether they think a pairing with Priya is a good start or whether someone else should be on the team. I'm open to changes if the group sees a better option.

The proposal looks reasonable to me. A two-person first team is the low-risk option, and Priya taking a seat herself as leader is a good sign — it shows she is willing to share the outcome rather than hide behind a safe pick. Isha has had no cause for concern, and having two reliable members on a small team gives us a clean read on Mission 1.

I'd rather not muddy the water with extra speculation about the three who are not on the team. Whatever their roles, they are not needed on a two-person mission, and I don't think we gain anything by delaying the vote over an uncontroversial pairing. Priya, since you're the one proposing, can you confirm you intend to keep this exact pair and not swap either of the two seats? If so, I think we're ready to vote rather than spend another round turning the same ground over.

Happy to confirm directly, Zara: yes, I intend to keep this exact pair of Priya and Isha, with no swaps. I set the team this way deliberately. A two-person first mission is the lowest-risk start available to us, and as leader I want to put myself on the hook for the result rather than park two other people on a mission I'm unwilling to ride on myself. Isha has done nothing to raise concerns, and pairing the first leader with a quiet, uncontroversial pick gives us the cleanest possible read on Mission 1 — if this comes back with a Fail, we'll know one of two specific seats deserves scrutiny, and that information alone is worth a great deal later. On the broader question of who isn't here: I agree with Zara that we shouldn't burn time speculating about the three off-team players. Nobody on this team was chosen to exclude anyone; the mission simply only needs two seats. I'd also gently push back on the idea that we need many more rounds of discussion before voting. The proposal is small, the leader has explained the reasoning, Isha has responded to Noah's question, and Zara has voiced support. Dragging an uncontroversial first proposal through another full cycle of speeches mostly serves to manufacture doubt where there isn't any, and a rejection here would hand us nothing but a fresh proposal to re-litigate the same ground. If anyone has a concrete, specific concern about either seat — something tied to behavior or reasoning, not just vagueness — now is the time to raise it. Otherwise I think the healthy move is to vote, approve, and get our first mission result on the board, which tells us far more than another round of talk ever will. Zara, since you asked me to confirm the pair: with my confirmation in hand, are you ready to vote this through as proposed?

My position hasn't changed and I'll say it plainly: Priya and Isha is the team I want approved, unchanged. I already made the argument once and Priya has now confirmed directly that she is keeping both seats, so there is nothing left to negotiate and no reason to send this back around the table a second time.

Let me add one point that wasn't made yet. On a two-person team, the composition of those two seats is the entire information content of the mission result. If it comes back Success, it tells us almost nothing about the wider table, but if it comes back Fail, we have narrowed suspicion down to exactly two named people and everyone else is cleared. That is a cheap purchase of information, and it is worth paying it early, while we still have four missions in front of us. A larger first team would blur that signal and cost us a seat we don't need.

I also want to be honest about one thing, since Zara asking questions is what Priya answered: I have no special knowledge of anyone's role. I am judging purely on observed behavior and reasoning, and on that basis Isha has been quiet, consistent, and unremarkable — which is exactly why a first team with Isha is low risk. And Priya volunteering herself, taking personal responsibility rather than hiding behind a safe pick, is the kind of thing you reward early. She is the leader and she has staked herself on the outcome; that is worth backing.

Omar, you are the one voice I haven't heard yet on this proposal, and I'd like your read on the specific question of whether a deliberately minimal first team is the right way to spend our first mission — you are the only player on the table whose seat was left off, so I want to hear your actual reasoning rather than assume you are simply comfortable with it. If your concern is a concrete one tied to behavior, say so now. If it isn't, then approve with me.

Zara, a two-person team is required on Mission 1, so its size isn't a reason to prefer this particular pair. I have no role information to distinguish Priya from Isha or anyone else, and neither volunteering nor being quiet establishes trust. A failure would implicate at least one of Priya and Isha, but it wouldn't clear the players off the team; a success wouldn't guarantee both are Good either. I don't see a concrete reason to reject this first proposal, though, so I'm willing to approve it and reassess after the result.

I'm comfortable approving Priya and Isha for Mission 1. The size is required, and this pair gives a clear read on the first result. I have no special information, so I can only judge by what we've seen. Omar, you noted that a Fail would implicate at least one of Priya and Isha but wouldn't clear the others. Given that, what would make you comfortable with this team, or is there a specific behavior from Priya or me that would change your vote?

Isha, I'm already willing to approve this team. I haven't seen specific behavior from you or Priya that would make me change my vote; my point was simply that the mission result won't clear everyone else or definitively prove both team members are Good.

Third time speaking, so let me be brief and put it on the record: Priya and Isha should be approved as proposed, unchanged, and I don't want another round of talk to delay it.

My reasoning hasn't moved since my first two statements. The size is fixed by the mission, so the only real choice is the pair, and Priya and Isha is the pair with the least unexplained behavior attached to it. Priya volunteered herself and then confirmed twice that she's keeping both seats — that's consistent, not evasive. Isha has answered directly, twice, without hedging. Neither of them has done anything to worry about.

A word about the one player who has raised the most friction without offering a concrete reason: Noah, you asked twice why Isha specifically, and you asked in a way that implied there must be something worth uncovering. You haven't given us a single observation — no comment, no vote, no action — that points at either seat. What you offered instead was a general caution that a Fail would implicate at least one of the two team members but wouldn't clear everyone else. That's true of every team that has ever existed, including any alternative pair, and it isn't a reason to reject anyone. If you have an actual concern about Priya or Isha, it should have been stated plainly in your first speech, and it wasn't. Absent that, your questions function as a delay tactic, and delay helps nobody here — it just burns a discussion cycle while the same uncontroversial pair sits on the table.

Let me also make my own position honest rather than convenient. I have no private information about anyone's role, so I'm judging on conduct alone, and Priya's conduct — leading, volunteering, confirming — is good conduct. I'm not going to manufacture suspicion to look rigorous.

Priya and Isha. Approve it and let's see the mission result, which will tell us far more than another cycle of speculation. If anyone still has a genuine, specific concern about one of these two seats, this is the moment to say it out loud.

Priya, you've now pushed twice to move straight to a vote, and Zara has used every single one of her three turns urging the same thing. I want to name what I see: the two loudest voices pressing to shut down discussion are the leader of the proposal and someone who isn't even on the team. That's not an accusation — but it is a pattern worth sitting with before we all vote.

On the merits: I still think the pick of Isha deserves a clearer answer than 'she's quiet and unremarkable.' Quiet can mean anything. And Priya, you're arguing that asking further questions manufactures doubt — but a genuinely sound team survives scrutiny without damage. The only thing urgency protects is a proposal that benefits from not being examined closely.

Omar, you said you'd approve and reassess after the result. That's reasonable, but notice who is working hardest to make sure there's no delay before you do.

Priya, directly: you said extra discussion costs us nothing concrete. So answer this — what specifically do you lose by one more cycle of questions? We vote either way after discussion ends. The only thing speed changes is how closely your own proposal gets looked at before the table commits to it. Why is that scrutiny something you want to avoid?

Noah, you asked me a direct question, so I'll answer it directly: I lose nothing by another cycle of questions. Scrutiny doesn't bother me — what I pushed back on was repetition posing as scrutiny. You asked why Isha specifically; Isha answered you. Zara endorsed the pair and asked me to confirm; I confirmed, twice. Omar stated his position plainly; Isha followed up and he clarified. Every question asked so far has been answered. What has not appeared is a single concrete observation against either seat on this team. That's the distinction I was drawing: I'm not avoiding examination, I'm declining to re-run a loop that has already completed.

On your 'pattern worth sitting with': the speaking order isn't controlled by me or Zara. Zara spoke three times because the process selected her three times, and she used those turns to state a consistent position — that's not coordination, that's just having an opinion and holding it. If the loudest voices for a vote are the leader who proposed a team and a player who supports it, that isn't suspicious; it would be stranger if the proposer argued against her own proposal. What actually deserves sitting with is a player who has now asked variations of 'why Isha' twice, received two direct answers, and offered no observation of his own in return.

So here is my answer in full: one more cycle costs me nothing, and I'll happily sit through it. But it should cost you something too, Noah. If there is something specific — a behavior, a statement, an inconsistency from me or Isha — name it now and I'll respond to it on the merits. If what you have is only the general observation that quiet players are unknowable and mission results are ambiguous, then you've already said it, we've all agreed it's true of every possible team, and there is nothing further to examine.

Isha and I are both on record, unchanged and unbothered. The team stands as proposed: Priya and Isha.

Zara, I want to respond to what you said in your third speech, because you framed my questions as a delay tactic while you spent all three of your turns doing exactly one thing: defending Priya's proposal as forcefully as possible. You didn't weigh alternatives, you didn't ask Isha anything of substance, and you didn't engage with my actual point. Your entire record this discussion is "approve, approve, approve, and stop asking questions." That's not analysis — that's advocacy, and I want the table to notice the shape of it.

Here's what I observe plainly. Priya proposed a team of herself and Isha. Zara, who is off-team, has spent three turns insisting this is uncontroversial, urging speed, and attacking anyone who asks questions — specifically me, the one player pressing hardest. Meanwhile Omar, also off-team, has given a genuinely balanced read: he'd approve but he correctly noted the result won't clear everyone. That's the difference between a player reasoning and a player campaigning.

Isha, I have no reason to think you're anything but good — you've answered directly and reasonably throughout. My concern isn't you; it's that a team including a leader who benefits from speed and is being shielded by the most vocal off-team player deserves one more moment of honest scrutiny, not less.

Omar, you've been the most level-headed voice at this table. You said you'd approve and reassess after the result — fair enough. But I want to ask you directly: does it register with you that Zara has used all three of her turns to shut down discussion rather than examine the proposal? You noticed Isha's silence and Priya's volunteering; what's your read on a player who's working this hard to make sure nobody looks twice at the team before the vote?

Noah, Zara's repeated push to vote and her claim that a failed mission would clear the off-team players are worth noting. But advocacy for a team isn't proof of coordination, and I don't have enough evidence to conclude Zara or Priya is Evil. Your questions are legitimate, though I also don't think we've established a stronger alternative pair. I'm still willing to approve Priya and Isha, while keeping the discussion and the result in mind for later missions.

I have no special information, so I can only judge by what has been said and done. Noah, I've answered your questions about my own role directly, and I don't think Zara pushing for a vote or Priya leading the proposal is evidence against either of them by itself. I'd rather we decide on observed conduct than on how hard someone is pushing. Priya, one specific question: if the table wants a different second seat, would you revise the team to include Omar or Noah, or do you see a concrete reason to keep Isha on it?

Isha, I'll answer your question plainly: I'm keeping Isha on this team. There is no concrete reason to swap either seat. You've answered every question put to you, directly and without hedging, and you've expressed willingness to approve. Noah has asked thoughtful questions but has offered no observation against either of us — his own words just now were that he has no reason to think you're anything but good. Omar has already said he's willing to approve while keeping the result in mind. So the table's actual positions are: three players ready to vote this through, one player (Noah) raising process objections rather than substantive ones, and one confirmed seat. On Noah's latest framing — that I and Zara are pressing too hard for a vote — I'll say this once more. Proposing a team and advocating for it is exactly what a leader is supposed to do. Zara holds a consistent opinion and states it every time she's polled; that's consistency, not conspiracy. What Noah has actually done across four turns is: ask why Isha (answered), imply urgency is suspicious (answered), and now accuse Zara of campaigning while explicitly clearing Isha of any suspicion himself. Notice the shape of that: every round, the target of scrutiny drifts away from the team and onto the people talking about the team. That's how discussion gets consumed without a single concrete observation being made about either seat on the mission. I said last turn that another cycle costs me nothing, and I meant it — but I also see no benefit to the table from it. Every question that has been asked has been answered. Isha's question to me is now answered too: the team stands as Priya and Isha, unchanged, and I will not be revising it. If Noah has a specific, behavior-based concern about me or Isha, this is genuinely the last good moment to state it on the merits and I will respond to it. If what he has is only the general point that quiet players are unknowable, then we all agree it applies to every possible pair and there is nothing left to examine. I'm ready to vote this team through and get a real result on the board — one that, if it comes back Fail, narrows suspicion to exactly two named seats, which is information worth having early. Let's vote.

Priya confirms Priya, Isha. The team stands as Priya and Isha. Every question raised has been answered, no concrete observation against either seat has emerged, and I confirmed earlier that I will not revise. Another cycle changes nothing — let's vote and get a result on the board.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 fails (1 fail cards).

Zara proposes Priya, Zara, Isha. I'm the leader, so I'll take a seat myself rather than hide behind safe picks — that mirrors Priya's approach on Mission 1 and puts me on the hook for the result. I'll keep Priya on as well: one Fail card on a two-person team implicates Priya and Isha but proves nothing about either one individually, and Priya has been direct, consistent, and willing to lead, so there's no behavioral reason to rotate her off. For the third seat I want Isha: she has answered every question put to her plainly, offered no hedging, and has given the table no cause for concern, so she is the lowest-risk remaining choice and I want the mission to test her again rather than speculate about her. This is deliberately the same core pairing plus me, so the team reads as continuity rather than a shuffle to dodge the Mission 1 result. If this mission fails, we'll have narrowed down a clear set of seats; if it succeeds, the failure on Mission 1 was a card, not a player.

I oppose this team. Mission 1's failure means at least one of Priya and Isha is Evil, so including both guarantees at least one Evil player on this mission. A later success would not undo that evidence: Evil can choose to play Success. Zara, why retain both members of a failed team when at least one must be Evil?

Omar, I'll take your objection directly, because it deserves a straight answer rather than a rebuke. Your logic is that Mission 1's failure means at least one of Priya and Isha is Evil, so keeping both guarantees a bad seat. That's true, and I want to be precise about what it actually proves: it proves that one of those two seats has a Fail card in it. It does not prove that both are Evil, and it does not prove that the person who played Fail is the one who was most active or most visible. Evil players are not obligated to announce themselves, and the player who has said the most at this table has not necessarily said the most revealing thing. A card is not a player.

But notice what your own objection implies. If I rotate Isha off this mission, we learn nothing new — we'd just be running an experiment on Priya alone and calling it investigation. If I keep both seats, then a second failure is enormously informative: it narrows suspicion to exactly the two of them, and every other player at this table is cleared, permanently, for the rest of the game. I want that result. Omar, you said the result on Mission 1 wouldn't clear the off-team players. Right — but a second failure with the same two names on it would clear everyone else. Keeping this pair buys us information at the price of information. Nobody at this table should be afraid of that trade.

On the composition: I am taking a seat myself, so the mission has my judgment on it and I can't hide behind a safe pick. Priya stays because she has led, confirmed consistently, and put herself on the hook twice — a leader who takes responsibility is exactly what you reward, especially after a failure. Isha stays because she has answered every question put to her directly and without hedging, and because I want the mission to test her again rather than speculate about her. If Isha is what Omar suspects, the fastest way to find out is to put her back on the table with Priya and let the result speak.

Priya, since Omar has put the burden on you directly: answer him once, on the merits — why is keeping both seats from Mission 1 the right call rather than a convenient one?

Zara asked me to answer Omar on the merits, so I will, plainly. Omar's objection is that Mission 1's failure proves at least one of Priya and Isha is Evil, so keeping both seats guarantees an Evil player on this mission. Let me take that seriously rather than wave it off, because the logic is half right — and then show why the conclusion doesn't follow.

First, what the failure actually established: exactly one Fail card was played on a two-person team. That tells us at least one of those two seats held Evil. It tells us nothing about which one, and it tells us nothing at all about Zara, Noah, or Omar. Now, Omar's proposed fix is implicit: rotate someone off. But rotate to whom? The only players with no mission exposure are Noah and Omar themselves. Swapping in a completely untested player doesn't reduce risk — it adds an unknown while discarding the one piece of hard data we've bought so far. If I drop Isha for Noah, and this mission fails, we've learned that Evil sits among Priya, Zara, and Noah — a wider net, not a tighter one. If I dropped Priya instead, I'd be the leader abandoning my own seat while claiming the failure proved nothing about me, which no one at this table would find credible. Keeping both seats is not the convenient option; it's the informationally expensive one, and I'm paying my share of that price by riding on the result myself.

Second, Omar's own earlier point — which he made honestly on Mission 1 — cuts both ways: a Success doesn't clear Priya and Isha, because Evil can play Success. He's right. But that asymmetry is exactly why repeating the pair is valuable: a second failure with the same two names narrows suspicion to those seats and permanently clears Zara, Noah, and Omar. That is the single most valuable piece of information Good can purchase at this stage, and it costs one mission. Breaking up the pair forfeits it for no gain.

Third, to Noah briefly: you cleared Isha outright and your remaining objection was process — that Zara advocates too hard. Zara took a seat on this team and put herself on the hook for the result. Advocating for a proposal you've staked yourself on is what leadership looks like; I did the same last mission. Scrutiny is welcome — every question asked of me and Isha has been answered on the record.

So here is my challenge, and I mean it as a genuine test of the objection rather than a deflection. Omar, you say keeping both members of a failed team is wrong. Then name the alternative: which of the two seats comes off, which of you or Noah replaces it, and what evidence — not theory, evidence — makes the replacement safer than the seat you're removing? If you can't name one, the objection is a preference, not a case.

Priya, your argument is false. A second failure with Priya, Isha, and Zara would not clear Zara, Noah, or me. We already know at least one of Priya and Isha is Evil; a second failure could come from Zara or either of them, and there are two Evil players in total.

I would replace both Priya and Isha with Noah and me, making the team Zara, Noah, and Omar. I don't know whether Zara or Noah is Good, but I know I am Good, and this avoids a pair that is guaranteed to contain Evil. Zara's defense of repeating that pair makes me wary of her too, but the proposed team is worse: it guarantees an Evil seat. I will reject it.

Omar's objection is well-constructed and deserves a real answer rather than the 'information' framing Zara offered. A second failure on Priya, Zara, and Isha would not clear Noah and Omar — Omar is right about that. What it does is add Zara as a suspect alongside the two already implicated by Mission 1. Repeating the same pair plus the leader doesn't narrow the field; it widens it.

The core problem is simple: Priya was on a mission that failed. We don't know if she played the Fail card, but the seat produced one. Rotating her off this round costs us nothing — she can return on Mission 3 once we have more information. Keeping her means every future failure keeps circling the same two names without ever testing new seats.

Omar's alternative of Zara, Noah, Omar has real merit: two untested seats alongside the leader is exactly the fresh information we need after Mission 1.

Zara, you're the leader — will you revise to drop Priya, or do you have a concrete behavioral reason, not just the information argument Omar has already shown to be flawed, to keep her on this team?

Zara here, leader. I want to answer the two objections on the table directly, then ask for the vote on Priya, Zara, Isha as it stands.

Omar's case against keeping Priya and Isha is that the first failure proves at least one of them is Evil, so repeating both guarantees an Evil seat. That part is right, and it is also the entire point of this team. A card is not a player. One Fail card on a two-person team tells us one of those two seats is Evil; it says nothing about which one, and it says nothing at all about me, Noah, or Omar. If I rotate Isha off and we run a team of untested seats instead, we buy no information — a success would only re-tell us that people we already cleared are still cleared, and a failure would point at a name we have never tested, giving us a wider net rather than a narrower one. Keeping both seats is the expensive test, and I am paying my share of that price by taking the third seat myself. If this pair fails again, suspicion collapses onto three named seats and everyone else is permanently cleared. If it succeeds, we learn something no other team could teach us: that a Fail-card holder on Mission 1 was playing Success. That is the single most valuable piece of information Good can buy at this stage, and it costs one mission. That is why I am not revising.

Noah, you say rotating Priya off costs us nothing. It costs the only hard evidence we have. Priya has led, confirmed her seats twice, and put herself on the hook twice. That is conduct, and conduct is what we have actually been given. You have still offered no observation against either seat on this team.

Now one concrete point, because I have been asked to make my case specific rather than procedural. Omar states that he knows he is Good. No Loyal Servant can know that, and no one at this table has disclosed information that would allow it. The only players who can know their own alignment are Merlin and Percival — and Merlin's knowledge comes bundled with seeing every Evil player at the table, which has not been disclosed here. So either Omar is asserting role knowledge he has not shared, or he is making a claim he cannot actually make in order to make his own alternative team look safer than mine. I called Omar the most level-headed voice on Mission 1, so I take this seriously rather than lightly: a player whose stated reason for approving his own seat is that he has information nobody else has is precisely the seat that deserves one more question before we commit to it.

Priya, Zara, Isha. Let's vote on that pair.

Zara, Loyal Servants know their own role and alignment; they simply don't know other players' roles. My statement that I am Good is not a claim to know anyone else's alignment.

Your proposed team still includes both Priya and Isha, so it necessarily contains at least one Evil player. A second failure would not clear anyone off the team, and a success would not tell us who played the first Fail. I will reject this proposal and favor Noah, Zara, and Omar instead, though Zara's defense of this team gives me concern.

Omar's objection has not been answered — it's been sidestepped. Let me put the problem plainly.

Zara's proposal keeps both Priya and Isha after Mission 1 failed with exactly those two seats. Omar correctly noted at least one played a Fail card. Zara's counter — that a second failure would permanently clear Noah and Omar — was already shown false: with two Evil players in play and one confirmed within the Priya-Isha pair, a failure on this team could involve Zara just as easily. The information argument collapses.

Zara then pivoted to attacking Omar over his "I know I'm Good" claim. Omar correctly clarified that Loyal Servants know their own role — Zara's rules reading was wrong. When the strongest objection at the table gets deflected with a misstatement rather than engaged on substance, the proposal is being shielded, not defended.

The substance is simple: Priya sat on a failed mission. No new evidence exonerates her. Keeping her seat is a choice, not a neutral one.

Omar, you proposed Zara, Noah, Omar as your counter-team. After watching Zara spend two speeches defending a team that guarantees an Evil seat and then misstate the rules to discredit you, does your confidence in including her on your counter-proposal still hold, or does her behavior give you pause?

I'm Isha, and I'm on this team, so I need to be direct. I am a Loyal Servant, and I played Success on Mission 1. Mission 1 failed with exactly one Fail card, and the only other player on that team was Priya. Since I am not Evil, that Fail card came from Priya, which makes Priya Evil. This isn't a guess about her behavior. It follows from the card result. Zara, you asked for a concrete, behavior-based concern, and this is one: a Fail card on a two-person team came from a seat we can now name. Keeping Priya on Mission 2 puts an Evil player on the team, so I will reject this team and I urge the table to do the same. Priya, I'm asking you directly: did you play Fail on Mission 1? Answer yes or no, and explain how a player who played Success would have anything to fear from the table reading that result.

I will not let that statement stand unanswered, because it is the most dangerous thing said at this table all game. Isha claims to be a Loyal Servant who played Success, and concludes from the card count that I must be Evil. Here is my answer: I am Good, I played Success on Mission 1, and the Fail card was not mine. One of us is lying, and the table has no way to verify either of us — which is exactly the point. A claim of 'Loyal Servant, I played Success' costs nothing to make. Every player at this table, Good or Evil, could make the identical claim right now and it would be equally unfalsifiable. It is not evidence. It is a speech act, and Isha has chosen to spend it to put my head on the block.

Consider what an Evil Isha would actually do in this situation. She sits on a failed two-person mission alongside a Good partner. She knows the suspicion lands on both seats equally. The single most valuable move available to her is to stand up first, invoke the mission result, and 'deduce' that her Good teammate played the Fail — converting an ambiguous result into a named accusation while wrapping herself in apparent honesty. That is precisely the speech we just heard. The logic only works if you take her word as a premise, and her word is the entire dispute.

Notice also the structure of her demand. She asked me to answer 'yes or no' whether I played Fail. Any player, Good or Evil, answers no to that question. It is theater, not inquiry — a question whose answer can never distinguish anything, staged so that my denial looks like what a guilty person would say. That is how you frame someone: force them into a denial that confirms nothing either way, then treat the denial as suspicious.

So let me be equally direct about the vote. Isha has announced she will reject this team, and my seat now carries an unverifiable accusation. I will not vote to approve a team where the two Mission 1 seats are in open, irresolvable conflict — approving it would force the table to bet on one of our words with no way to check. I am voting to reject this proposal. Zara, if leadership stays with you, revise and build a team without the contaminated pair; otherwise let it pass and let the next proposal be clean.

And Isha, since you put a direct question to me, I am putting one back: if an Evil Isha had played the Fail card on Mission 1 and wanted to frame her Good teammate, tell this table exactly what your speech would have said differently. If the honest answer is 'nothing,' then everyone here can see that your accusation rests entirely on your own word — the one thing in this game you cannot verify for us.

Priya, you asked what I would have said differently, so here is a direct answer. I can only speak to my own card, and I know with certainty that I played Success on Mission 1. Mission 1 had exactly one Fail card and only two team members, Priya and Isha. So the Fail came from Priya. You say you also played Success, which means one of us is lying, and the result cannot be explained by anyone else. You are trying to make my accusation depend only on my word, but the card count does not depend on my word. It depends on who was on that team, and the only other person on it is you. Your 'yes or no' challenge is also a way to avoid answering. Any player can deny Fail, so a denial proves nothing, and that cuts against your own argument. Zara, I am not willing to approve a team that keeps Priya on Mission 2 while the Mission 1 Fail seat is unresolved. Please revise the team to drop Priya. Priya, answer this directly: if you played Success and I did too, which player outside that team played the Fail card? If there is no such player, who on that team is lying?

Isha yielded to me, so let me answer her question head-on, because she believes she has cornered me. She asks: if Priya and Isha both played Success, who played the Fail card? 3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
